In mathematics, specifically in [[functional analysis]] and [[Hilbert space]] theory, '''vector-valued Hahn–Banach theorems''' are generalizations of the [[Hahn–Banach theorem]]s from linear functionals (which are always valued in the [[real number]]s <math>\R</math> or the [[complex number]]s <math>\mathbb{C}</math>)  to linear operators valued in [[topological vector space]]s (TVSs).

==Definitions==

Throughout {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}} will be [[topological vector space]]s (TVSs) over the field <math>\mathbb{K}</math> and {{math|L(''X''; ''Y'')}} will denote the vector space of all continuous linear maps from {{mvar|X}} to {{mvar|Y}}, where if {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}} are normed spaces then we endow {{math|L(''X''; ''Y'')}} with its canonical [[operator norm]].

===Extensions===

If {{mvar|M}} is a vector subspace of a TVS {{mvar|X}} then {{mvar|Y}} has '''the extension property from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|X}}''' if every continuous linear map {{math|''f'' : ''M'' → ''Y''}} has a continuous [[Linear extension (linear algebra)|linear extension]] to all of {{mvar|X}}. If {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}} are [[normed space]]s, then we say that {{mvar|Y}} has '''the metric extension property from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|X}}''' if this continuous linear extension can be chosen to have norm equal to {{math|{{norm|''f''}}}}.

A TVS {{mvar|Y}} has '''the extension property from all subspaces of {{mvar|X}}''' (to {{mvar|X}}) if for every vector subspace {{mvar|M}} of {{mvar|X}}, {{mvar|Y}} has the extension property from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|X}}. If {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}} are [[normed space]]s then {{mvar|Y}} has '''the metric extension property from all subspace of {{mvar|X}}''' (to {{mvar|X}}) if for every vector subspace {{mvar|M}} of {{mvar|X}}, {{mvar|Y}} has the metric extension property from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|X}}.

A TVS {{mvar|Y}} has '''the extension property'''{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}} if for every locally convex space {{mvar|X}} and every vector subspace {{mvar|M}} of {{mvar|X}}, {{mvar|Y}} has the extension property from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|X}}.

A [[Banach space]] {{mvar|Y}} has '''the metric extension property'''{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}} if for every Banach space {{mvar|X}} and every vector subspace {{mvar|M}} of {{mvar|X}}, {{mvar|Y}} has the metric extension property from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|X}}.

'''1-extensions'''

If {{mvar|M}} is a vector subspace of normed space {{mvar|X}} over the field <math>\mathbb{K}</math> then a normed space {{mvar|Y}} has '''the immediate 1-extension property from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|X}}''' if for every {{math|''x'' ∉ ''M''}}, every continuous linear map {{math|''f'' : ''M'' → ''Y''}} has a continuous linear extension <math>F : M \oplus (\mathbb{K} x) \to Y</math> such that {{math|{{norm|''f''}} {{=}} {{norm|''F''}}}}. We say that {{mvar|Y}} has '''the immediate 1-extension property''' if {{mvar|Y}} has the immediate 1-extension property from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|X}} for every Banach space {{mvar|X}} and every vector subspace {{mvar|M}} of {{mvar|X}}.

===Injective spaces===

A [[locally convex topological vector space]] {{mvar|Y}} is '''injective'''{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}} if for every locally convex space {{mvar|Z}} containing {{mvar|Y}} as a topological vector subspace, there exists a continuous [[Projection (linear algebra)|projection]] from {{mvar|Z}} onto {{mvar|Y}}.

A [[Banach space]] {{mvar|Y}} is '''1-injective'''{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}} or a '''{{math|''P''<sub>1</sub>}}-space''' if for every Banach space {{mvar|Z}} containing {{mvar|Y}} as a normed vector subspace (i.e. the norm of {{mvar|Y}} is identical to the usual restriction to {{mvar|Y}} of {{mvar|Z}}'s norm), there exists a continuous [[Projection (linear algebra)|projection]] from {{mvar|Z}} onto {{mvar|Y}} having norm 1.

==Properties==

In order for a TVS {{mvar|Y}} to have the extension property, it must be [[Complete topological vector space|complete]] (since it must be possible to extend the [[identity map]] <math>\mathbf{1} : Y \to Y</math> from {{mvar|Y}} to the completion {{mvar|Z}} of {{mvar|Y}}; that is, to the map {{math|''Z'' → ''Y''}}).{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}}

===Existence===

If {{math|''f'' : ''M'' → ''Y''}} is a continuous linear map from a vector subspace {{mvar|M}} of {{mvar|X}} into a complete Hausdorff space {{mvar|Y}} then there always exists a unique continuous linear extension of {{mvar|f}} from {{mvar|M}} to the closure of {{mvar|M}} in {{mvar|X}}.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}}<ref>{{harvnb|Rudin|1991|p=40}} Stated for linear maps into [[F-space]]s only; outlines proof.</ref>
Consequently, it suffices to only consider maps from closed vector subspaces into complete Hausdorff spaces.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}}

==Results==

Any locally convex space having the extension property is injective.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}}
If {{mvar|Y}} is an injective Banach space, then for every Banach space {{mvar|X}}, every continuous linear operator from a vector subspace of {{mvar|X}} into {{mvar|Y}} has a continuous linear extension to all of {{mvar|X}}.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}}

In 1953, [[Alexander Grothendieck]] showed that any Banach space with the extension property is either finite-dimensional or else {{em|not}} [[Separable space|separable]].{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}}

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}} |math_statement=
Suppose that {{mvar|Y}} is a Banach space over the field <math>\mathbb{K}.</math>
Then the following are equivalent:
# {{mvar|Y}} is 1-injective;
# {{mvar|Y}} has the metric extension property;
# {{mvar|Y}} has the immediate 1-extension property;
# {{mvar|Y}} has the center-radius property;
# {{mvar|Y}} has the weak intersection property;
# {{mvar|Y}} is 1-complemented in any Banach space into which it is norm embedded;
# Whenever {{math|Y}} in norm-embedded into a Banach space <math>X</math> then identity map <math>\mathbf{1} : Y \to Y</math> can be extended to a continuous linear map of norm <math>1</math> to <math>X</math>;
# {{mvar|Y}} is linearly isometric to <math>C\left(T, \mathbb{K}, \|\dot{}\|_{\infty}\right)</math> for some compact, [[Hausdorff space]], [[extremally disconnected space]] {{mvar|T}}. (This space {{mvar|T}} is unique up to homeomorphism).

where if in addition, {{mvar|Y}} is a vector space over the real numbers then we may add to this list:
#<li value="9"> {{mvar|Y}} has the binary intersection property;
# {{mvar|Y}} is linearly isometric to a complete [[Archimedean ordered]] [[vector lattice]] with order unit and endowed with the order unit norm.
}}

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}} |math_statement=
Suppose that {{mvar|Y}} is a {{em|real}} Banach space with the metric extension property.
Then the following are equivalent:
# {{mvar|Y}} is [[Reflexive space|reflexive]];
# {{mvar|Y}} is [[Separable space|separable]];
# {{mvar|Y}} is finite-dimensional;
# {{mvar|Y}} is linearly isometric to <math>C\left(T, \mathbb{K}, \|\cdot\|_{\infty}\right),</math> for some discrete finite space <math>T.</math>
}}

==Examples==

'''Products of the underlying field'''

Suppose that <math>X</math> is a vector space over <math>\mathbb{K}</math>, where <math>\mathbb{K}</math> is either <math>\R</math> or <math>\Complex</math> and let <math>T</math> be any set.
Let <math>Y := \mathbb{K}^T,</math> which is the product of <math>\mathbb{K}</math> taken <math>|T|</math> times, or equivalently, the set of all <math>\mathbb{K}</math>-valued functions on {{mvar|T}}.
Give <math>Y</math> its usual [[product topology]], which makes it into a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[locally convex]] TVS.
Then <math>Y</math> has the extension property.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=341–370}}

For any set <math>T,</math> the [[Lp space]] <math>\ell^{\infty}(T)</math> has both the extension property and the metric extension property.
